stem: Jonas needs an empty file called `todo.txt` in the current directory. Which command creates it if it doesn’t exist yet?

options.rationale: `mkdir` would create a directory with that name.
`cat` only reads a file, so it reports an error when the file is missing.
`touch` creates an empty file when the name is new.
`cp` needs a source and a destination, and the source doesn’t exist.

explanation: `touch NAME` creates an empty file, or, if the file exists, only updates its modification time. It can take several names at once.

stem: The file `notes.txt` already contains text. What does `touch notes.txt` do to it?

options.text: It keeps the content and updates the modification time
options.rationale: `touch` only changes the timestamps of an existing file.

options.text: It empties the file so that it can be written again
options.rationale: `touch` never removes the content.

options.text: It creates a second file named `notes.txt` beside it
options.rationale: Two files cannot share a name in one directory.

options.text: It fails with an error because the name already exists
options.rationale: `touch` works fine on existing files.

explanation: For an existing file, `touch` leaves the data alone and sets the modification time to now. Only for a new name does it create an empty file.

stem: Mira wants the directory chain `levels/world1/boss` created in one command, but `levels` doesn’t exist yet. Which command works?

options.rationale: Without `-p`, `mkdir` fails because the parent `levels/world1` doesn’t exist.
`mkdir` has no `-r` option.
`touch` makes files, not directories, and doesn’t create the parents.
`-p` creates missing parent directories as needed.

explanation: `mkdir` creates one directory and refuses when a parent is missing. `-p` (parents) creates the whole chain and doesn’t complain about directories that already exist.

stem: Jonas wants to delete the directory `old`, but only if it is empty, so nothing is lost by accident. Which command should he use?

options.rationale: `rm -r` deletes the directory with everything in it.
`rmdir` removes a directory only when it is empty.
This deletes everything below `old` without asking.
That is not a way to remove a directory.

explanation: `rmdir` is the safe way to remove directories: if anything is still inside, it fails with “Directory not empty”. `rm -r` removes the contents too.

stem: Mira runs `cp backup backup2` on a directory and gets “omitting directory”. What does she have to add?

options.text: The `-f` option, to force the copy of directories
options.rationale: `-f` forces overwriting of files, but doesn’t make `cp` descend.

options.text: The `-r` option, to copy the directory and everything inside it
options.rationale: `cp -r` copies recursively.
This is not how `cp` is told to copy directories.

options.text: A trailing slash after the target name
options.rationale: A slash alone doesn’t change that `cp` skips directories.

explanation: By default `cp` copies only files. With `-r` (recursive) it also copies directories and their contents. `mv` needs no such option.

stem: Ada wants to rename `slime.png` to `blob.png`, with no copy left behind. Which command does this?

options.rationale: `cp` leaves the original `slime.png` in place.
The arguments are reversed: this would rename `blob.png`.
`rm` deletes both names.
Moving a file to a new name in the same place is how files are renamed.

explanation: There is no separate rename command in the basic toolkit: `mv OLD NEW` renames. Source first, destination second.

stem: Jonas deletes a file with `rm` by mistake. What happens to the file?

options.text: It is removed at once, and there is no trash to restore it from
options.rationale: The command line has no recycle bin.

options.text: It is moved to a hidden trash folder in his home directory
options.rationale: `rm` doesn’t move anything to a trash folder.

options.text: It is kept in `/tmp` and restored with `undelete`
options.rationale: No such restore command exists, and `/tmp` isn’t a backup.

options.text: It is only hidden, and `ls -a` brings it back
options.rationale: `rm` doesn’t rename files; they are really removed.

explanation: `rm` deletes the directory entry for good. Check the names (an `echo` in front of the command shows what a wildcard expands to) before pressing Enter.

stem: Which command deletes the directory `old` together with everything that is inside it?

options.rationale: `rmdir` fails when the directory is not empty.
Without `-r`, `rm` refuses to remove a directory.
`-r` makes `rm` remove directories recursively.
This asks before each removal, but on a directory it fails like plain `rm`.

explanation: `rm -r` descends into directories and removes everything. Add `-i` to be asked before each removal, and be very careful with `-f`.

stem: Ada copies `hero1.png` to `hero2.png`, and `hero2.png` already exists. What does `cp` do by default?

options.text: It asks whether to overwrite the file first
options.rationale: It asks only when `-i` is given.

options.text: It stops with an error, because the name is taken
options.rationale: It doesn’t refuse; the destination is replaced.
Without `-i`, `cp` replaces an existing destination without asking.

options.text: It adds a number to the name of the new file
options.rationale: `cp` doesn’t pick a new name unless `--backup` is given.

explanation: `cp` and `mv` overwrite existing files without a warning. `-i` asks first, and `-n` never overwrites.

stem: Mira’s art folder holds both `notes.txt` and `Notes.txt`. What is true?

options.text: They are two different files, because Linux file names are case sensitive
options.rationale: Upper and lower case letters make different names.

options.text: Only one of them can exist, so the second would replace the first
options.rationale: On Linux both can exist side by side.

options.text: Both names refer to the same file
options.rationale: That happens on some other systems, not on Linux.

options.text: The shell shows an error whenever both names are used in one command
options.rationale: There is no such restriction.

explanation: File names, directory names, commands and options are all case sensitive on Linux. `notes.txt`, `Notes.txt` and `NOTES.TXT` are three names.

stem: The directory is called `art`, but `cd Art` prints “No such file or directory”. What is the reason?

options.text: Directories can only be entered with an absolute path
options.rationale: Relative paths such as `art` work fine.

options.text: `cd` can’t change into a directory that Mira owns
options.rationale: Owning a directory doesn’t stop `cd`.

options.text: The capital letter is read as an option of `cd`
options.rationale: Only words starting with a dash are options.

options.text: The name `Art` is a different name from `art`
options.rationale: Directory names are case sensitive.

explanation: A name that differs only in case doesn’t exist. Tab completion helps, as it fills in the exact spelling.

stem: Which pattern matches `boss1.png` and `boss2.png`, but not `boss10.png`?

options.rationale: The `*` also matches the two characters in `10`.
The `?` stands for exactly one character.
This needs two characters between `boss` and `.png`, so only `boss10.png` matches.
This excludes `boss1.png`.

explanation: `?` matches exactly one character, `*` matches any number of characters, including none, and `[abc]` matches one character from a set.

stem: What does the pattern `hero[13].png` match?

options.rationale: That would need a range such as `[1-3]`.
The brackets match one character from the list, either 1 or 3.
The brackets match just one character, so the two digits do not both appear.

options.text: A file that is literally named `hero[13].png`
options.rationale: The shell treats the brackets as a pattern if matching files exist.

explanation: `[13]` is a set of one character. `[1-3]` is a range from 1 to 3, and `[!13]` is any character that is not 1 or 3.

stem: When Mira types `rm *.tmp`, which part of the system turns `*.tmp` into a list of file names?

options.text: The `rm` program, when it reads its arguments
options.rationale: `rm` receives the already expanded list of names.

options.text: The kernel, when it opens the files
options.rationale: The kernel doesn’t know about patterns.

options.text: The terminal emulator, when she presses Enter
options.rationale: The terminal only sends the typed characters on.
Globbing is done by the shell, so every command gets the same behaviour.

explanation: The shell expands wildcards before the command runs. This is why quoting the pattern, `"*.tmp"`, hands the star to the command unchanged.

stem: Ada wants to copy every `.png` file in the current directory into the directory `backup`. Which command does this?

options.rationale: The shell expands `*.png`, and `backup`, as the last argument, is the destination.
The destination must come last, so this would copy `backup` into a PNG file name.
The quotes stop the expansion, so `cp` looks for a file literally named `*.png`.
No destination is given, so this fails.

explanation: With several sources, `cp` expects the destination directory last. An unquoted `*.png` is replaced by all matching names.

stem: Which of these commands refuse to work on a directory unless the option `-r` is given? (Choose TWO.)

options.rationale: It skips directories unless told to copy recursively.
It won’t remove a directory without `-r`.
It moves a directory like any other file.
Its whole job is directories.
It only works on the timestamps of names and takes no `-r`.

explanation: `cp -r` and `rm -r` are recursive. `mv` needs no option for directories, and `mkdir` and `rmdir` work on directories anyway.

stem: Which statements about case sensitivity on Linux are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: `Notes.txt` and `notes.txt` can exist in the same directory
options.rationale: They are different names.
Options are case sensitive too.
Command names are case sensitive, so `LS` isn’t found.

options.text: Only directory names are case sensitive, not file names
options.rationale: Both are.
The names differ, so `cd` fails.

explanation: Everything is case sensitive: file names, directory names, command names and options.

stem: Which names does the pattern `hero?.png` match? (Choose TWO.)

options.rationale: One character, `1`, stands in for the `?`.
One character, `2`, stands in for the `?`.
Two characters between `hero` and `.png`.
The `?` needs exactly one character, so the name must not be missing it.
The extension differs from `.png`.

explanation: `?` matches exactly one character: not none and not two. Matching is case sensitive as well.

stem: Which patterns match the file name `slime.png`? (Choose THREE.)

options.rationale: Any name that ends in `.png`.
The `?` stands for the `l`.
The name starts with a lower-case letter.
It needs one more character before `.png`.
The extension differs from `.png`.
It must start with a character that is not `s`.

explanation: Test each pattern in order: `*` matches any run of characters, `?` exactly one, `[a-z]` one letter in the range, and `[!s]` anything but `s`.

stem: Type the command that creates an empty file named `todo.txt`.
explanation: `touch` creates the file when the name is new.

stem: Complete the command so that the whole chain `levels/world1/boss` is created in one step.
explanation: `-p` creates the missing parent directories too, and doesn’t complain about existing ones.

stem: Complete the command so that the directory `art` is copied with everything inside it to a new directory `art2`.
explanation: The recursive option makes `cp` copy a directory tree. `-R` and `-r` mean the same for `cp`, unlike for `ls`.

stem: In the directory `art`, type the command that renames `notes.txt` to `todo.txt`.
explanation: `mv` renames when the destination is a new name in the same directory.

stem: Complete the command so that it lists every file in `art` whose name ends in `.png`.
explanation: The shell expands `art/*.png` into the matching names before `ls` runs.

stem: In the directory `art`, type the command that removes the empty directory `backup`, and only if it is empty.
explanation: `rmdir` refuses to remove a directory that still has content, which makes it the safe choice.

stem: In the directory `art`, type the command that deletes the directory `backup` and everything inside it.
explanation: `-r` makes `rm` recursive. The extra `-f` isn’t needed and removes the safety checks.

stem: Type what this command prints.
explanation: The brackets match one character that is either 1 or 3, so `hero2.png` isn’t included. `echo` prints the expanded names.

stem: Type what this command prints.
explanation: Each pattern is expanded on its own. `boss?.png` skips `boss10.png`, since the `?` is only one character, and `hero?.png` matches all three heroes.

stem: The art folder has two notes files. What does this command print?

options.rationale: `cat` prints the files in the order given, and `Notes.txt` is named first.
The two names are different files with different content.
`cat` prints `Notes.txt` first and then `notes.txt`, which are two different files.

options.text: cat: notes.txt: No such file or directory
options.rationale: Both files exist, since the names differ by case.

explanation: The two names don’t clash because case matters. `cat` joins the files in the order of its arguments.

stem: Jonas misspells the extension in capitals. Type what this command prints.
output: cat: readme.MD: No such file or directory
explanation: `readme.MD` is a different name from `readme.md`, so `cat` reports that there is no such file.

stem: Type what this command prints.
command: cd art; mkdir -p one/two/three; ls -R one
explanation: `mkdir -p` creates the chain, and `ls -R` lists each directory in turn, separated by a blank line.

stem: Mira moves one sprite onto another. What does this command print?
command: cd art; mv hero1.png hero2.png; cat hero2.png

options.rationale: `mv` replaced the old `hero2.png`; its content is gone.
The files are not merged; the second one is replaced.
`mv` silently overwrites the destination, so `hero2.png` now holds the content of `hero1.png`.

options.text: mv: cannot move 'hero1.png' to 'hero2.png': File exists
options.rationale: `mv` overwrites existing files unless it is told otherwise with `-i` or `-n`.

explanation: Without `-i` (ask) or `-n` (never overwrite), `mv` and `cp` replace an existing destination without a warning.

stem: What does this command print?
command: cd art; echo hello > todo.txt; touch todo.txt; cat todo.txt

options.rationale: `touch` leaves the content alone for an existing file; only the time stamp changes.
`touch` is happy to work on existing files.
`touch` does not append anything.
`cat` prints the content of the file, not its name.

explanation: `echo hello > todo.txt` creates the file with one line. `touch` afterwards only changes its modification time, so `cat` shows `hello`.

stem: Ada removes the single-digit boss sprites with a wildcard. What does this command print?
command: cd art; rm boss?.png; ls boss*

options.rationale: Those are the files that were removed; the `?` matches one character.
`rm` has deleted two of these.

options.text: ls: cannot access 'boss*': No such file or directory
options.rationale: `boss10.png` still matches `boss*`.
`boss?.png` removes only names with one character after `boss`, so `boss10.png` stays.

explanation: The `?` matches exactly one character, so `boss1.png` and `boss2.png` are deleted and the two-digit `boss10.png` survives.
